codeExamples.title: Basic Decision Tree
codeExamples.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1000, n_features=10, n_informative=5)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, min_samples_split=10)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'Train accuracy: {tree.score(X_train, y_train):.3f}')
print(f'Test accuracy: {tree.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

codeExamples.title: Visualize Tree
codeExamples.code:
from sklearn.tree import plot_tree, export_text
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Visual plot
plt.figure(figsize=(20, 10))
plot_tree(tree, filled=True, feature_names=[f'feat_{i}' for i in range(10)], 
          class_names=['0', '1'], rounded=True)
plt.title('Decision Tree Visualization')
plt.show()

# Text representation
tree_rules = export_text(tree, feature_names=[f'feat_{i}' for i in range(10)])
print(tree_rules)

codeExamples.title: Random Forest
codeExamples.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import numpy as np

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, 
                           min_samples_split=5, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'RF Train: {rf.score(X_train, y_train):.3f}')
print(f'RF Test: {rf.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

# Feature importance
importances = rf.feature_importances_
indices = np.argsort(importances)[::-1]

print('\nFeature ranking:')
for i in range(10):
    print(f'{i+1}. Feature {indices[i]}: {importances[indices[i]]:.4f}')

codeExamples.title: Cross-Validation
codeExamples.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
import numpy as np

# Decision Tree CV
tree_scores = cross_val_score(tree, X, y, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
print(f'Tree CV: {tree_scores.mean():.3f} (+/- {tree_scores.std():.3f})')

# Random Forest CV
rf_scores = cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
print(f'RF CV: {rf_scores.mean():.3f} (+/- {rf_scores.std():.3f})')

codeExamples.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
codeExamples.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import randint

param_dist = {
    'n_estimators': randint(50, 500),
    'max_depth': randint(3, 20),
    'min_samples_split': randint(2, 20),
    'min_samples_leaf': randint(1, 10)
}

rf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
rand_search = RandomizedSearchCV(rf, param_dist, n_iter=50, cv=5, 
                                random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
rand_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'Best params: {rand_search.best_params_}')
print(f'Best CV score: {rand_search.best_score_:.3f}')
print(f'Test score: {rand_search.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

codeExamples.title: Out-of-Bag Error
codeExamples.code:
# OOB: Free validation (no need for separate validation set!)
rf_oob = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, oob_score=True, 
                                random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
rf_oob.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'OOB Score: {rf_oob.oob_score_:.3f}')  # Unbiased estimate
print(f'Test Score: {rf_oob.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

# OOB predictions
oob_preds = rf_oob.oob_decision_function_
print(f'OOB predictions shape: {oob_preds.shape}')  # (n_train, n_classes)

quiz.question: Decision Tree'de Gini impurity ne ölçer?
options: Node purity: How mixed are classes? 0=pure, 0.5=max impurity
quiz.explanation: Gini: 1 - Σ(pᵢ²). Measures class mixture! Pure node (all one class): Gini=0. Equal classes: Gini=0.5 (binary). Why important: Training finds splits that minimize impurity → maximize purity. Lower Gini after split = better split! Alternative: Entropy (similar, slightly different math). Both work well. Gini slightly faster to compute.

quiz.question: Random Forest neden single decision tree'den daha iyi?
options: Ensemble reduces overfitting & variance: Averages many trees → more stable!
quiz.explanation: Single tree: High variance (small data change → very different tree), overfits easily. Random Forest: Bagging + random features → decorrelates trees. Each tree sees different data/features → different mistakes. Average predictions → errors cancel out! Result: Lower variance, better generalization. Bias-variance tradeoff: Slightly higher bias, much lower variance. Overall: Better! Ensemble wisdom > individual.

quiz.question: Random Forest'ta feature importance nasıl hesaplanır?
options: Sum of impurity decreases from splits using that feature, averaged across trees
quiz.explanation: Feature importance: For each feature, sum all impurity decreases when splitting on that feature. Across all trees! High importance = feature used often + splits data well. Low importance = rarely used or poor splits. Applications: Feature selection (drop low importance), interpretability (which features matter?). Warning: Biased toward high-cardinality features. Use permutation importance for unbiased estimate.

quiz.question: Decision Tree hangi durumlarda iyi çalışmaz?
options: Linear relationships: Needs many splits to approximate line. Inefficient!
quiz.explanation: Trees excel at: Non-linear, interactions, different feature scales. Struggle with: Linear relationships! Must approximate line with many horizontal/vertical splits → inefficient, deep tree. Example: y = 2x + 3 → tree needs 100s of splits. Linear regression: 1 line. Also poor: Extrapolation (can't predict beyond training range), smooth functions (step-wise approximation). When to avoid: Linear data (use linear models), need smooth predictions, online learning.

quiz.question: Bootstrap aggregating (bagging)'in amacı nedir?
options: Reduce variance: Train on different random samples → decorrelate predictions!
quiz.explanation: Bagging: Bootstrap (sample with replacement) + Aggregate. Each tree sees ~63% unique samples, 37% repeated. Effect: Trees trained on slightly different data → different predictions. Aggregate (vote/average): Reduces variance! Individual predictions fluctuate, average is stable. Why works: Errors uncorrelated → cancel out. Signal correlated → reinforces. Bias unchanged (each tree has same bias), variance reduced significantly. Foundation of Random Forests!

quiz.question: Tree pruning neden yapılır?
options: Reduce overfitting: Remove branches that don't improve validation performance
quiz.explanation: Full tree: Often overfits (perfect training accuracy, poor test). Pruning: Remove branches that hurt generalization. Two types: (1) Pre-pruning: Stop early (max_depth, min_samples_split). (2) Post-pruning: Grow full tree, then remove branches. Method: Cost-complexity pruning. Trade-off: Accuracy vs tree size. Sklearn: Use max_depth, min_samples. Manual pruning less common (Random Forest handles overfitting via ensemble). Pruning = regularization for trees!

commonMistakes.why: Unlimited depth → perfect training accuracy, terrible test! Memorizes noise, every leaf = 1 sample.
commonMistakes.fix: Always set max_depth! Start with 3-10, tune via cross-validation. Also: min_samples_split (5-20), min_samples_leaf (1-5). For Random Forest: Can go deeper (ensemble handles overfitting), but still limit (20-30 max). Monitor: Training vs test accuracy gap.

commonMistakes.why: Single tree: High variance, unstable. Small data change → completely different tree. Unreliable predictions!
commonMistakes.fix: Use Random Forest! Minimal overhead, much better performance. Or gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM). Single tree: Only for interpretation/exploration. Production: Always ensemble. Exception: Very interpretable model required (medical diagnosis) → prune carefully.

commonMistakes.why: Imbalanced classes → tree biased toward majority. Minority class ignored! Poor recall on rare class.
commonMistakes.fix: Solutions: (1) class_weight='balanced' (penalize minority errors more). (2) Sample weight per class. (3) SMOTE oversampling. (4) Stratified sampling. (5) Adjust decision threshold. Random Forest: class_weight='balanced_subsample'. Monitor: Per-class metrics, not just accuracy!

commonMistakes.mistake: Too few trees in Random Forest
commonMistakes.why: 10-20 trees → high variance still. Benefits of ensemble not realized. Performance worse than could be.
commonMistakes.fix: Use 100-500 trees minimum! More trees → better (with diminishing returns). No overfitting from too many trees (only slow). Sweet spot: 100-300 for most datasets. Large datasets: 500-1000. Computationally cheap: Always err on more trees. Monitor: OOB error vs n_trees.

commonMistakes.why: Miss opportunity for insights! Feature importance shows what model learned. Critical for debugging, trust.
commonMistakes.fix: Always check feature importance! Sanity check: Important features make sense? Unexpected feature → investigate. Applications: (1) Feature selection (drop low importance). (2) Debugging (why predictions wrong?). (3) Domain validation (model using right info?). Plot: Bar chart of top 10-20 features.

commonMistakes.why: Trees can't extrapolate! Only predict within training range. Outside → predicts nearest leaf. Fails completely on new range.
commonMistakes.fix: Don't use for: Time series forecasting far future, physics simulations (need extrapolation). Warning: If test data outside training range → tree fails. Check: Feature ranges in train vs test. Alternatives: Parametric models (linear, exponential), neural networks (limited extrapolation).

commonMistakes.why: One-hot encoding + trees = inefficient! Trees can handle categorical directly (sklearn: ordinal encode). One-hot creates many features, tree searches all.
commonMistakes.fix: For tree-based models: Ordinal encode categorical features (0, 1, 2, ...). Tree will find best splits! One-hot: Wastes computation, dilutes feature importance. Exception: LightGBM, CatBoost have native categorical support (even better!). Only use one-hot for: Linear models, neural networks.

title: Decision Trees & Random Forests
description: Decision Trees: Tree-based models for classification & regression! Internal nodes = feature tests, branches = outcomes, leaves = predictions. Training: Recursively split data to maximize purity (Gini, entropy). Advantages: Interpretable (visualize tree), handles non-linear data, no feature scaling needed. Disadvantages: Overfits easily, unstable (small data change → different tree). Random Forests: Ensemble of decision trees! Train many trees on random subsets (bagging), average predictions. Reduces overfitting, more stable. Feature importance via tree splits. Applications: Credit scoring, medical diagnosis, feature selection. Fast training & inference. Foundation for gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM).

content.level0_basic: Decision Tree: Series of yes/no questions! Like game '20 questions'. Example: Predict if person buys product: Q1: Age > 30? Yes → Q2: Income > 50k? Yes → Buy! No → Don't buy. No → Q3: Has kids? ... Build tree: Find best questions (features) that split data into pure groups. Gini impurity: How mixed is group? Pure = all same class. Training: Top-down, greedy. Pick best split at each step. Stop when pure or max depth. Prediction: Follow path from root to leaf. Fast! Problems: (1) Overfits: Memorizes training data. (2) Unstable: Small change → different tree. Random Forest solution: Train 100 trees on different data samples, vote! Majority wins. Wisdom of crowds. More stable, less overfit. Each tree slightly different → ensemble powerful!
content.level1_beginner:
**Decision Tree Algorithm:**

```
1. Start at root (all data)
2. For each node:
   a. Try all features, all split points
   b. Calculate impurity after split
   c. Choose split with lowest impurity
3. Create child nodes with split data
4. Recursively repeat for children
5. Stop when:
   - Node is pure (all same class)
   - Max depth reached
   - Too few samples
```

**Impurity Measures:**

```
Gini Impurity:
  Gini = 1 - Σ(pᵢ²)
  where pᵢ = proportion of class i
  
  Pure node: Gini = 0
  50-50 split: Gini = 0.5
  
Entropy (Information Gain):
  H = -Σ(pᵢ·log₂(pᵢ))
  
  Pure: H = 0
  Maximum: H = log₂(classes)

Both work similarly!
```

**Random Forest:**

```
1. Bootstrap: Sample data with replacement
2. For each tree:
   a. Use bootstrap sample
   b. At each split: Random subset of features
   c. Train decision tree
3. Prediction:
   - Classification: Majority vote
   - Regression: Average

Typical: 100-500 trees
Feature subset: √d (classification) or d/3 (regression)
```

**Feature Importance:**

```
For each feature:
  Importance = Σ (impurity decrease from splits using feature)
  
Higher importance → More useful for prediction

Random Forest: Average importance across all trees
```
content.level2_application:
**Scikit-learn Decision Tree:**

```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import plot_tree

# Load data
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)

# Train
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'Accuracy: {tree.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

# Visualize
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 10))
plot_tree(tree, filled=True, feature_names=['sepal_len', 'sepal_wid', 'petal_len', 'petal_wid'])
plt.show()
```

**Random Forest:**

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import numpy as np

# Train forest
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=5, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'RF Accuracy: {rf.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

# Feature importance
importances = rf.feature_importances_
feature_names = ['sepal_len', 'sepal_wid', 'petal_len', 'petal_wid']

for name, imp in sorted(zip(feature_names, importances), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True):
    print(f'{name}: {imp:.3f}')
```
content.level4_expert:
**Gradient Boosted Trees (Foundation for XGBoost):**

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Hyperparameter tuning
param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200, 500],
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 7],
    'learning_rate': [0.01, 0.1, 0.3],
    'subsample': [0.8, 1.0]
}

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)
grid = GridSearchCV(gb, param_grid, cv=5, scoring='accuracy', n_jobs=-1)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'Best params: {grid.best_params_}')
print(f'Best score: {grid.best_score_:.3f}')

# Feature importance
best_model = grid.best_estimator_
importances = best_model.feature_importances_
```

**XGBoost (Production):**

```python
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

# Convert to DMatrix (XGBoost format)
dtrain = xgb.DMatrix(X_train, label=y_train)
dtest = xgb.DMatrix(X_test, label=y_test)

# Parameters
params = {
    'max_depth': 5,
    'eta': 0.1,  # learning rate
    'objective': 'multi:softmax',
    'num_class': 3,
    'eval_metric': 'merror'
}

# Train
model = xgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round=100, 
                  evals=[(dtest, 'test')], early_stopping_rounds=10)

# Predict
preds = model.predict(dtest)
print(classification_report(y_test, preds))
```

whatIsIt: Decision Tree: Hierarchical model with binary splits. Each internal node tests feature, branches represent outcomes, leaves contain predictions. Training: Greedy, top-down. At each node, find best feature/threshold to split data (maximize purity). Impurity: Gini or entropy. Stops when pure, max depth, or min samples. Prediction: Traverse tree from root to leaf. Random Forest: Ensemble of trees. Bootstrap aggregating (bagging): Each tree trained on random sample with replacement. Random feature selection at each split. Prediction: Majority vote (classification) or average (regression). Reduces variance, more robust. Feature importance: Sum of impurity decreases. Foundation for boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost).
whyNeeded: Why use Decision Trees: (1) Interpretable: Visualize and understand decisions. Medical, legal domains need explainability. (2) No preprocessing: Handles categorical data, missing values, different scales. (3) Non-linear: Captures complex patterns. (4) Fast: Training O(n·d·log n), prediction O(log n). (5) Feature selection: Shows important features. Why Random Forest: (1) Reduces overfitting: Single tree unstable. Ensemble stabilizes. (2) High accuracy: Often matches neural networks! (3) Handles high-dimensional data. (4) Out-of-bag (OOB) error: Free validation. (5) Parallelizable: Trees independent. Applications: Credit scoring, fraud detection, medical diagnosis, customer churn, feature engineering. When not to use: Need probability calibration (trees give rough probabilities), online learning (need retraining), very high-dimensional sparse data (deep learning better).
realWorldAnalogy: Decision Tree = Flowchart diagnosis! Doctor: 'Temperature > 38°C? Yes → Cough? Yes → Prescribe antibiotics.' Each question = node, answer = branch, diagnosis = leaf. Build tree: Find most informative questions. Gini = How decisive is this question? Good question splits sick/healthy clearly. Bad question: 50-50 both ways. Training: Doctor learns from 1000 cases. Which symptoms best separate diseases? Random Forest = Medical panel! One doctor might be biased (overfit one symptom). Solution: 100 doctors, each sees random patient subset, considers random symptoms. Vote on diagnosis! Majority wins. Wisdom of crowds. More reliable than single doctor. Each doctor slightly different perspective → robust decision. Feature importance: Which symptoms mentioned most often across all doctors? Those are critical!

stepByStep: 1. Start with all data at root
a. If stopping criteria met, make leaf
c. Split data into left/right children
a. Bootstrap sample: n samples with replacement
b. Build tree with random feature subsets
algorithm.complexity: Training: O(n·d·log(n)·T) where T=trees, n=samples, d=features. Single tree: O(n·d·log n). Prediction: O(log(n)·T). Space: O(nodes·T). Typically log(n)=depth. RF trains in parallel!
